examples.label: Brute-force a known user over XML-RPC (fast, multi-threaded)

notes: The xmlrpc method is far faster than wp-login because it accepts many auth attempts per request; if xmlrpc.php is blocked, fall back to wp-login. Confirm the username with --enumerate u first so you only spray passwords.

recommended.note: Use the cracked admin creds to plant a theme webshell.
Automate the same admin->shell path with Metasploit.

name: WPScan - Password Brute Force (xmlrpc)
description: Brute-forces a WordPress account through the xmlrpc endpoint (faster and quieter than wp-login). Recovered admin creds lead to code execution via the theme editor.

defense.why_it_works: WordPress /wp-login.php does not rate-limit by default and returns distinct errors for invalid username vs incorrect password, enabling username enumeration. WPScan uses this to efficiently brute-force credentials.
defense.prerequisites: Valid username list from wpscan-enum. HTTP access to /wp-login.php. No CAPTCHA or rate-limiting present.
defense.impact: Compromised admin credentials grant full control: theme/plugin editor access for webshell upload, user management, complete site data exfiltration.
defense.detection: High volume POST requests to /wp-login.php from one IP. Failed login events in WordPress logs or WordFence. Authentication log spikes.
defense.artifacts: WordPress authentication logs (failed logins) | WordFence alert emails | Web server POST request logs to /wp-login.php
defense.splunk_spl:
index=web sourcetype=access_combined uri_path="/wp-login.php" status=401 OR status=403 OR (method=POST status=200)
| stats count by clientip, bin(_time, 1m)
| where count>20
defense.elastic_kql: event.category:web AND url.path:"/wp-login.php" AND (http.response.status_code:(401 OR 403) OR http.request.method:POST)
defense.sentinel_kql:
W3CIISLog
| where csUriStem =~ "/wp-login.php"
| summarize attempts=count(), fails=countif(scStatus in (401,403)) by cIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where attempts > 20
| sort by attempts desc
// WordPress login/xmlrpc brute force
defense.sigma_rules: web_login_bruteforce (high-rate POST to /wp-login.php from one IP)
defense.prevention: Install WordFence or Limit Login Attempts to lock accounts after N failures. Require CAPTCHA on login. Enable 2FA. Disable XML-RPC if not needed.
defense.misconfiguration: WordPress /wp-login.php publicly accessible with no rate-limiting, no CAPTCHA, and distinct error messages enabling username enumeration. xmlrpc.php also enabled.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# WordPress default
# POST /wp-login.php -> distinct error per username vs password
# No lockout after N failures
# xmlrpc.php enabled
defense.evasion: Brute-force via xmlrpc.php multicall method (bypasses login page protections). Use random User-Agent. Add throttle delay.

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review IIS Web Server logs, Windows Security Event Log, Web proxy logs for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Brute-forces a WordPress account through the XML-RPC endpoint:
  wpscan                   the WordPress scanner
  --password-attack xmlrpc  use xmlrpc (faster/quieter than wp-login)
  -t 20                    20 threads
  -U <user> -P <wordlist>  the target user and password list
  --url http://<url>       the site
Recovered admin creds lead to code execution via the theme editor.
